terms.grammar: ferō with the adverb aegrē; the thing as object, or the accusative and infinitive
evidence: Cic. Tusc. 4.17.40: aegrē ferre repulsam cōnsulātūs (Lewis & Short), s.v. ferō
terms.comment: Also molestē ferre and, more strongly, graviter ferre.
Traupman’s phrase. Every word is classical; we have found no classical instance of the phrase.

terms.gloss: take it hard that, be upset that
evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.1.152: hoc ēreptum esse, graviter et acerbē ferre (Lewis & Short s.v. ferō)

terms.comment: Classically cordī esse is to be dear to someone, to please (quod tibi magnopere cordī est, Lucil., Lewis & Short s.v. cor); we have found no classical instance of cordī habēre for “take to heart”.

sources: Lewis & Short: aegre · Lewis & Short: fero
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
